messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun Mehta was seven years old when the violence in his childhood home shifted from occasional shouting to terrifying, unpredictable aggression. He would sit on the bottom step of the staircase, gripping the wooden railing until his knuckles whitened, watching his father’s shadow stretch across the hallway as glass shattered against plaster. What frightened him most was the suddenness of it; there was no warning, only the roar of his father’s rage and the heavy, final slam of the front door. His mother never reported the abuse, and the authorities were never involved. The people responsible had faced no consequences, and the household simply learned to move in silence. Arjun had come to believe that he was fundamentally powerless to stop bad things from happening, a conviction that settled into his bones long before he could articulate it. As an accountant, Arjun navigated the predictable world of quarterly audits and financial ledgers, yet his daily environment became a minefield of invisible threats. When he tried to discuss the past during early counseling sessions, he found his throat tight and his hands trembling, completely unable to put the frightening event into words. Instead, it surfaced as a nonverbal memory. A heavy file folder dropping to the carpeted floor at his firm would instantly trigger that memory without warning. The terror on recall was not merely a recollection; it flooded his system, his body on alert, muscles locking, breath catching in his throat. His deep-seated belief that he was helpless, coupled with the knowledge that justice had never been served, kept his nervous system permanently braced for impact. This conviction directly fueled his physical reactivity, turning ordinary office stimuli into perceived dangers. Whenever that wordless terror breached his awareness, his physiology would surge into physical reactivity, every nerve ending snapping taut. The exhausting toll of this constant hypervigilance slowly drained his capacity for joy. He was superalert and watchful across every workday, scanning the open-plan office for signs of conflict and interpreting a colleague’s raised voice during a budget review as an omen of disaster. His body on alert state and relentless hypervigilance meant he was constantly scanning for danger, and this hyper-alertness easily captured ordinary office stimuli, instantly triggering a nonverbal memory without warning. The steady erosion of his well-being, his conviction that he used to be a happy person but now was always miserable, pulled those fragmented childhood scenes to the forefront of his mind. The sheer weight of those inescapable flashbacks reinforced his negative appraisal that he was powerless to change his internal state, deepening his conviction that life would always remain miserable. The exhausting toll of being superalert and watchful across every workday confirmed his hopelessness; the constant tension left no room for the happiness he had once possessed, cementing his belief that he could not stop bad things from happening to him. His avoidance of late-night audits and his refusal to attend client dinners fractured his professional standing and eventually contributed to the slow dissolution of his marriage, his wife unable to bridge the distance created by his constant readiness to flee. Now, at thirty-six, Arjun sits in a therapist’s office, finally ready to confront the architecture of his own fear. He admits that he has become a ghost in his own life, terrified that seeking help will strip away the very vigilance that has kept him surviving. Yet, he hopes, perhaps for the first time in decades, to find a way to quiet the alarm in his chest and reclaim the peace he thought he had lost forever.
